title: Bonaventure's mind
hook: the Franciscan way of thinking: love goes further than knowledge

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony and the fish: a preacher refused by a city, preaching to the water. Your line was preach anyway. Did you say your kind sentence, and could you leave the result alone? Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

Francis never wrote a book of theology. He told his brothers to work with their hands, to preach peace, to bear a locked gate patiently. Then the brotherhood grows, and some of the friars end up in lecture halls. One of them teaches at the university of Paris, in a world of disputations, where a question is argued for and against, point by point. He's a man trained to argue. So what does a friar like that do with a founder who preached to birds? Does he leave the stories behind? Today, the scholar who tried to think the Franciscan way.
screen: `A FOUNDER WHO WROTE NO THEOLOGY.` → `A FRIAR IN A LECTURE HALL.` → `DOES HE LEAVE THE STORIES?`

segments.voice: His name is Bonaventure. He taught in Paris, he led the Franciscan order, and he wrote a life of Francis. And he wrote a short book with a long name, The Journey of the Mind into God. He tells us how it began. He went up to La Verna, the mountain where Francis had seen a vision of a seraph, an angel with six wings, and there, looking for peace, he started thinking about those six wings. He came to see them as six steps of a journey toward God. First you find God's traces in the world outside: in stones, in plants, in birds, in everything that is. Then you turn inward and find God's image in your own mind, in memory, understanding and love. Then you look above the mind, to God himself. It's a ladder of thought, and it's hard going. But before you set out, Bonaventure gives a warning. Don't think reading is enough without the anointing of grace, he says, or thinking without devotion, or study without wonder, or knowledge without love. And at the top of the ladder, he does something surprising. He tells the mind to let go of its thinking. If you want to know how this happens, he says, ask grace, not learning. Ask desire, not understanding. Ask the groaning of prayer, not the diligence of study. Ask the Bridegroom, not the teacher. It's the same thing Saint Paul tells the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth." Bonaventure didn't throw away knowledge. He spent his life teaching and writing. But in this book, knowledge reaches an edge, and love keeps going. In his hands, the Franciscan way of thinking runs like this: think as hard as you can, then let love carry you the rest of the way.
screen: `SIX WINGS, SIX STEPS TO GOD.` · `OUTSIDE, INSIDE, ABOVE.` · `ASK GRACE, NOT LEARNING.` · `KNOWLEDGE STOPS; LOVE KEEPS GOING.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE PUFFETH UP; BUT CHARITY EDIFIETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love where you can't understand. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you don't understand. A choice they made that baffles you. A way of seeing the world that's not yours. Notice if part of you wants to figure them out first, to solve them, before deciding how to feel. If so, let that rest. You can stay puzzled. Now, without understanding them any better, wish them well. Their health, their peace, their good. If you pray, you can hold them before God, puzzle and all. If you don't, simply let goodwill go out toward them on the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bonaventure's mind. A scholar's ladder of thought toward God, that ends by letting go of thinking and asking for love. Today's word.
Your line: love goes further. Today, when you hit the edge of what you understand about someone, do them one kindness from right there. Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Franciscans and other Catholics read Bonaventure's Journey of the Mind into God as a guide to prayer, and the Church honors him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

myth: he taught in Paris and wrote volumes. he warned against knowledge without love, not knowledge.
Bonaventure read the six wings of Francis's seraph as six steps toward God
outside in the world, inside in the mind, then above the mind.

fork.setup: you're Bonaventure, at the top of your ladder of thought. how do you say the last step is reached?
options: by asking grace, desire and prayer, not learning.
by arguing it out with a better teacher.
fork.reveal: he tells the mind to ask grace, not learning; desire, not understanding; the Bridegroom, not the teacher.

original.note: Latin: a guide for a journey; the first word of the book's Latin title.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scholar's head full of arguments.
what it means: a ladder of thought toward God that ends by handing the last step to love.
what a scholar hears: the Journey of the Mind into God, built on Francis's six-winged seraph, ending in a passing-over beyond the intellect.
